summary:
We developed an interactive web application that helps users explore fire hotspot records across the MODIS–VIIRS transition. Using NASA FIRMS observations, our workflow estimates historical monthly counts on the Suomi NPP VIIRS scale through country-specific statistical models.

Linked maps, a fire calendar and a situation dashboard help researchers and decision-makers examine seasonal patterns and regional anomalies while distinguishing satellite observations from model-based estimates. The project addresses the risk of interpreting differences between sensors as changes in fire activity.
details:
PROBLEM AND USERS

MODIS and VIIRS observe fire hotspots at different spatial resolutions and sensitivities. Combining their raw counts can introduce artificial discontinuities in historical records. Our project helps researchers, civil defense teams and land managers explore these records with clearer distinctions between observations and estimates.

DATA PREPARATION

We downloaded NASA FIRMS hotspot records and normalized timestamps, coordinates, satellite identifiers and sensor attributes. We preserved source detections and aggregated monthly counts by country and satellite. The processing workflow uses Python, DuckDB and CSV/Parquet outputs.

HARMONIZATION METHOD

For Argentina, we compared six regression configurations combining Quasi-Poisson and Negative Binomial families with proportional, exponential and power mean functions. Quasi-Poisson with a power mean function achieved the lowest in-sample mean absolute error.

We fitted the selected model structure separately for each country and MODIS source satellite. Aqua is the preferred input, with Terra used when Aqua is unavailable for a country/month. The method estimates monthly counts on the Suomi NPP VIIRS scale rather than matching individual fire pixels.

Predicted monthly counts are stored separately from observed counts. For the historical spatial series, pre-2012 estimates are distributed through weights assigned to source detections; from 2012 onward, the historical workflow uses observed S-NPP detections.

INTERACTIVE APPLICATION

The application includes an interactive map, a month-by-year fire calendar, linked time-series charts, regional selection and CSV export. Users can select an area and period to investigate seasonal patterns and compare sensor records.

The Situation Room presents recent hotspot activity alongside seasonal expectations, regional anomalies and a priority queue. It supports investigation and planning rather than providing a validated fire forecast.

EVALUATION AND LIMITATIONS

For Argentina / Aqua to S-NPP, the selected regression was fitted and evaluated on 168 paired months from January 2012 through December 2025. Its MAE was 3,287.39 hotspots per month and its RMSE was 4,970.02 hotspots per month.

These are in-sample metrics, not independent estimates of future predictive accuracy. Country-level models may hide local differences in vegetation, fire characteristics and observation conditions. Independent temporal validation, vegetation-aware models and regional calibration are future improvements.

The application's calendar-month ratio diagnostic is separate from this regression evaluation.

TECHNOLOGY AND REPRODUCIBILITY

The application uses Python, Dash, Plotly, DuckDB, Parquet and Shapely, with Docker hosting on Hugging Face Spaces. The repository contains extraction notebooks, regression code, application code and reproduction instructions.
